Writing a property and expecting the paired output on the same node to be a different value — input and output are two faces of the same stored property.

dynamicPorts.description: Input and output ports derive from node parameters: configured headers and query parameters become inputs; response mappings become outputs.

enrichment.summary: HTTP Request: fetches a URL on demand, delivering the parsed response, status code and success/failure signals.
enrichment.description: The straightforward HTTP client: set `url` (plus method/headers/body via its configuration), fire `fetch`, and read `response` (parsed body, untyped), `responseHeaders`, and `statusCode`. `success`/`failure` split the outcome, with `error` describing failures; `cancel` aborts an in-flight request.
enrichment.whenToUse: One-off or simple API calls where the response can be consumed directly or handed to a Function/Script for shaping. Prefer the REST node when an endpoint is reused enough to deserve declared ports; prefer a cloud function when credentials must stay off the client.

ports.response: Untyped output with the parsed body — being '*', it connects anywhere; downstream correctness is on the author.
ports.statusCode: Number level with the HTTP status of the last response.
ports.failure: Signal; wire error display/retry here, with `error` carrying the message.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Header and body inputs are runtime-registered from the node's method/headers configuration; only the core trigger/result surface is static.
patterns: `failure` → Condition `eval` with `result` → error text `visible`: errors as levels, not pulses.

enrichment.summary: Parent Component Object: reads the enclosing parent component's instance-scoped object from inside a child component.
enrichment.description: Parent Component Object opens the same per-instance store as the parent's Component Object, from within a child. Properties declared on the node become value outputs that update reactively as anything writes the parent's object; `changed` fires per write. This is how reusable child components (controls, toolbars, wizard steps) participate in their host's state without dedicated ports for every value.
enrichment.whenToUse: Child components that are conceptually part of their parent and share its state — wizard controls, list toolbars. For unrelated components use Objects by id or events; for one-off values a Component Input is more explicit.

ports.changed: Signal; the parent's object was written by anyone.
ports.fetch: Signal; re-emit current values on demand.

enrichment.summary: Animate To Value: tweens its output toward whatever targetValue currently is, with duration, delay and easing.
enrichment.description: Animate To Value is the current general-purpose tween. Whenever `targetValue` changes, `currentValue` animates from wherever it is to the new target over `duration` ms with the chosen `easingCurve`; `atTargetValue` fires on arrival. It is retarget-safe: changing the target mid-flight redirects the animation smoothly instead of jumping.
enrichment.whenToUse: Smoothing any numeric change: positions, opacity, blend values for Color Blend. It supersedes the deprecated Transition/Animation nodes. For multi-property, state-shaped animation use States with transitions.

ports.targetValue: Number level; each change starts (or redirects) the tween toward it.
ports.currentValue: Number level streaming the animated value — wire to the visual input being animated.
ports.atTargetValue: Signal; the tween arrived. Sequence follow-ups here.

patterns: Boolean state → (boolean→number cast) → `targetValue`: a two-state tween in one wire.
`currentValue` → Color Blend `blendValue`: animated color transitions.

enrichment.summary: Single-line or multi-line text entry control with label, icon, placeholder and focus handling; outputs the text as the user types.
enrichment.description: The Text Input control renders an editable text field (or text area, or email/number/password/URL input, chosen by the `type` enum). Its main product is `onTextChanged` (display name 'Text'), a string output that updates continuously as the user types; the `textChanged` signal fires on every such change and `onEnter` fires when the user presses Enter. Text can also be written programmatically: the `startValue` (Text) input holds the field text, and the `set` signal applies it on demand. Optional label and icon sections, per-state styling and focus control (`focus`/`blur` signals, `focusState` output) are built in.
enrichment.whenToUse: Any free-text entry. Use `type` instead of separate nodes for email/number/password fields. For multi-line text set `type` to textArea. ports.onEnter: Signal; fires when the user presses Enter while the field is focused.
ports.startValue: String input ('Text'). When `set` is unconnected a new value applies immediately; when `set` is connected the value is held until `set` fires. While the field has focus, programmatic writes are ignored so they cannot fight the user's typing.
ports.set: Signal; applies the pending `startValue` to the field.
ports.focus: Signal; gives the field keyboard focus (`blur` removes it).
ports.type: Enum: text, textArea, email, number, password or url. textArea renders a multi-line editor.

The catalog list is the superset; the editor shows the subset matching current parameters.

`onEnter` → the same action as the submit button's `onClick`: keyboard-friendly forms.
A stored value → `startValue` with a load signal → `set`: prefill a form when data arrives.
antiPatterns: Polling the text with a timer — `onTextChanged` is already live; wire it directly.
Wiring `textChanged` (signal) where the text string is wanted; use `onTextChanged`.

enrichment.summary: External Link: opens a URL outside the app — same tab or new tab — when its signal fires.
enrichment.description: External Link leaves the app: when `do` fires, the browser navigates to `link`, in a new tab when `openInNewTab` is true. It performs no in-app routing and returns nothing — the page is left (or a tab opened) and that is the whole contract.
enrichment.whenToUse: Documentation links, third-party checkout, mailto/tel URLs. For anything inside the app use Navigate or Navigate To Path, which keep SPA state alive.

ports.link: The absolute URL (or mailto:/tel: scheme) to open.

antiPatterns: Pointing External Link at the app's own routes — the full page reload throws away application state that Navigate would keep.

enrichment.summary: Logs a user into the cloud backend with username and password, establishing the session the User node reflects.
enrichment.description: Log In sends the current `username` and `password` (string values) to the cloud backend when `login` (Do, signal) is triggered. On success the returned session is stored in the browser (it persists across reloads), the app-wide user service switches to the logged-in user — which updates every User node and fires their Logged In signal — and `success` (signal) fires. On a bad login or network problem `error` (string value) is set with the message and `failure` (signal) fires; nothing about the current session changes.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action node behind a login form. To read who is logged in, or to react to session changes, use the User node; to create an account use Sign Up (which also logs the new user in); to end the session use Log Out.

ports.login: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); performs the login after pending input updates, so username/password wired from inputs are current.
ports.success: Signal; fires once the session is established. Typical next step: navigate to the logged-in page.
ports.failure: Signal; fires on rejected credentials or request failure. Show `error` to the user.
ports.error: String value holding the backend's error message from the last failed attempt.

patterns: Text Input `text` → `username`/`password`, Button `onClick` → `login`, `success` → navigation: the standard login form.
`error` → a Text node's `text`: surface backend messages like 'Invalid username/password' directly.
antiPatterns: Driving logged-in UI from this node's `success` signal alone — state belongs to the User node's `authenticated` boolean, which also covers sessions restored on reload.

enrichment.summary: Ends the current user session on the cloud backend and clears it from the browser.
enrichment.description: Log Out ends the current session when its `login` input (displayed 'Do', signal) is triggered: the backend session is revoked, the stored session is removed from the browser, and the app-wide user service switches to logged-out — updating every User node (`authenticated` becomes false) and firing their Logged Out signal. `success` (signal) fires when this completes; `failure` (signal) fires with `error` (string value) set if the request fails.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action behind a log-out button or menu item. To react to the session ending (e.g. navigate to the login page), listen on this node's `success` or the User node's Logged Out signal.

ports.login: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); note the file-key name is `login` even though this node logs out.
ports.success: Signal; fires once the session has ended.
ports.failure: Signal; fires if the logout request fails. Read `error` for the message.

patterns: Button `onClick` → `login` (Do), `success` → navigate to the public/login page.

enrichment.description: Sign Up creates a user from the current `username`, `password` and optional `email` (string values), plus one input per custom property on the User class, when `signup` (Do, signal) is triggered. On success the new account is immediately logged in — the session is stored in the browser, every User node updates, their Logged In signal fires — and `success` (signal) fires. On failure (e.g. username taken) `error` (string value) is set and `failure` (signal) fires, and no account is created.
enrichment.whenToUse: The action node behind a registration form. For signing in an existing user use Log In; for editing the signed-in user's properties later use Set User Properties.

ports.signup: Signal input (displayed 'Do'); performs the sign-up after pending input updates so all field values are current.
ports.success: Signal; fires once the account exists and the user is logged in — no separate Log In step is needed.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the backend rejects the sign-up. Show `error` to the user.
ports.error: String value holding the backend's error message, e.g. an already-taken username.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: The editor generates one value input per custom property in the User class schema (stored as `prop-<name>`, typed from the schema; built-ins like username, password, email and system fields are excluded). These set the new user's properties at creation time.
patterns: Text Inputs → `username`/`password`/`email`, Button `onClick` → `signup`, `success` → navigate into the app: the standard registration form.
Fill `prop-<name>` inputs at sign-up for properties every account must have, instead of a follow-up Set User Properties call.
antiPatterns: Triggering Log In from `success` — sign-up already establishes the session.

ssr.note: Sessions live in browser storage; a server render always sees a logged-out user.

dynamicPorts.description: Property outputs include one port per custom user property in addition to the built-in ones.

enrichment.summary: Reads the currently signed-in user: id, username, email, custom properties, and an authenticated boolean, kept live across session changes.
enrichment.description: User mirrors the current session's user. Its value outputs — `id`, `username`, `email` (strings) and one output per custom property on the User class — always reflect the signed-in user, and `authenticated` (boolean) is true exactly while a user is signed in. The node tracks the app-wide user service: it updates when Log In or Sign Up succeeds, when a stored session is restored, and when Log Out runs or the session is lost, so a single connection from `authenticated` can gate an entire logged-in UI. `changed` (signal) fires when the user's data changes. Triggering `fetch` (signal) re-reads the user from the server, firing `fetched` on completion or `failure` with `error` (string value) set. It also works inside cloud functions, where it reflects the calling user's session.
enrichment.whenToUse: The one node to read who is logged in and their properties, anywhere in the app. It performs no actions — pair it with Log In, Sign Up, Log Out and Set User Properties for those.

ports.authenticated: Boolean value; true while a user is signed in. The canonical driver for logged-in/logged-out UI, including sessions restored on page load.
ports.fetch: Signal input; re-fetches the current user from the server (e.g. after another device may have changed it). While connected, the node suppresses its automatic per-change outputs and updates on fetch instead.
ports.fetched: Signal; fires when a `fetch` round-trip completes successfully.
ports.changed: Signal; fires when any property of the current user's data changes locally.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Beyond the static ports, the editor generates one value output per custom property in the User class schema (stored as `prop-<name>`, typed from the schema) plus a `changed-<name>` signal per property (built-ins authData/password/username/email are excluded — username and email have static outputs). In the browser it additionally registers the signal outputs `loggedIn` (Logged In), `loggedOut` (Logged Out) and `sessionLost` (Session Lost), which fire on the corresponding session transitions; these do not exist in the cloud runtime.
patterns: `authenticated` → a Group's `visible` (and through an inverter to the login form): one boolean drives both faces of the UI.
`loggedOut`/`sessionLost` signal outputs → navigation to the login page: handle forced sign-outs globally.
antiPatterns: Storing the user id in your own variable at login time — read `id` from this node instead so restored and switched sessions stay correct.

enrichment.summary: Deprecated: confirms a user's email address using an emailed token. Superseded by cloud-function-based flows.
enrichment.description: Verify Email submits `username` and `token` (string values, the token coming from the verification email) to the backend when `verify` (Do, signal) is triggered; `success`/`failure` (signals) and `error` (string value) report the outcome. It is marked deprecated in the runtime — the source directs new work to cloud functions, where a component called via CloudFunction2 verifies the token and marks the address confirmed server-side.
enrichment.whenToUse: Do not use in new graphs — implement email verification in a cloud function called via CloudFunction2 instead.

enrichment.summary: Responsive multi-column layout: distributes its children into columns whose relative widths come from a layout string.
enrichment.description: Columns lays out its visual children in a grid of columns described by `layoutString`: a space-separated list of relative widths, so '1 2 1' means three columns where the middle one is twice as wide as the outer ones (default '1 2 1'). Children fill the columns in order and wrap into further rows when there are more children than columns. `marginX` (Horizontal Gap) and `marginY` (Vertical Gap) set the spacing in pixels (default 16), and `minWidth` (Min Column Width) makes the layout responsive: when the container gets too narrow to honour the minimum, columns fold away and content reflows into fewer, wider columns. `direction` flips the fill order between row and column, and `justifyContent` aligns partial rows. The node warns in the editor if `layoutString` is bound to a non-string.
enrichment.whenToUse: Card grids, dashboards, magazine-style layouts — anywhere content should reflow across a variable number of columns. For a fixed row or column of items a plain Group with `flexDirection` is simpler; for one instance per data record put a For Each inside the Columns.

ports.layoutString: String value of space-separated relative widths, e.g. '1 2 1'. The number of entries is the column count; each entry is that column's share of the width.
ports.minWidth: Number value in px (Min Column Width, default 0): below this per-column width the layout folds columns away and reflows — this is what makes the grid responsive.
ports.marginX: Number value in px (Horizontal Gap) between columns.
ports.marginY: Number value in px (Vertical Gap) between wrapped rows.

patterns: Responsive card grid: layoutString '1 1 1' + `minWidth` ~200 so three columns collapse to two, then one, as the viewport narrows.
For Each inside Columns: repeated component instances distribute across the columns automatically.

enrichment.summary: Displays a glyph from a project icon font, or an image, at a given size — tintable via color for font icons.
enrichment.description: Icon renders a single icon. With `iconSourceType` (Type) set to 'icon' (the default) it shows a glyph from an icon set enabled in the project — `iconIconSource` (Icon Source) identifies the glyph (a CSS class plus code) and `iconColor` tints it, `iconSize` setting the font size in pixels. ports.iconSourceType: Enum value (Type): 'icon' (glyph from a project icon set, default) or 'image'. Chooses which source/color ports are shown.
ports.iconIconSource: Icon value (Icon Source): the glyph, picked from the project's enabled icon fonts; stored as class + code.
ports.iconColor: Color value; tints font-icon glyphs only — image sources keep their own colors.
ports.iconSize: Number value in px: font size for glyphs, width and height for image sources.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Declared-port-groups keyed on `iconSourceType`: 'icon' exposes `iconIconSource` and `iconColor`, 'image' exposes `iconImageSource`; `iconSize` and `iconSourceType` are always shown. (An internal `useIcon` flag defaults to true and has no editor input on this node.)
patterns: Icon + Text in a row Group: the standard labeled-metadata row in cards and lists.
Bind `iconColor` from state (e.g. a Condition's boolean via a Switch/States color) to reflect status.

enrichment.summary: Create Record (BYOB): inserts a record into a self-hosted backend class, returning the new record and its id.
enrichment.description: The bring-your-own-backend Create Record posts a new record with the property values on its schema-generated inputs when `create` fires. `success` delivers `record` (the created object) and `recordId`; `failure` delivers a structured `error`. `loading` is a boolean level for progress UI. Unlike the classic cloud-data family, BYOB results do not live-update — pair writes with an explicit re-fetch of any Query Data feeding the UI.
enrichment.whenToUse: Creating records against a self-hosted/BYOB backend. On the managed cloud backend use Create New Record (NewDbModelProperties) instead.

ports.recordId: The new record's id — hand it to Update/Delete Record or store it for navigation.
ports.loading: Boolean level, true while the request is in flight.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Class choice and per-property inputs are generated from the backend schema (runtime-discovered); the static surface is only the trigger and result ports.
patterns: `success` → the list query's `fetch`: BYOB writes refresh reads explicitly.

enrichment.summary: Delete Record (BYOB): removes a record from a self-hosted backend by id when triggered.
enrichment.description: When `delete` fires, the record targeted by the node's id input is removed from its class on the BYOB backend. `success`/`failure` (with structured `error`) report the outcome and `loading` spans the request. Deletion is final, and dependent Query Data nodes see the change only on their next `fetch`.
enrichment.whenToUse: Destructive removal on a self-hosted backend. On the managed cloud backend use Delete Record (DeleteDbModelProperties). Prefer a soft-delete flag via Update Record when undo matters.
enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Class choice and the id input are schema-generated (runtime-discovered).

dynamicPorts.description: Filter/parameter ports are derived from the configured query definition.

enrichment.summary: Query Data (BYOB): fetches records from a self-hosted backend class on demand into a records array.
enrichment.description: The bring-your-own-backend query: when `fetch` fires it runs the configured query against the BYOB backend and emits `records` (array), `count`, `totalCount`, and `firstRecord`. `loading` covers the request window; `success`/`failure` sequence follow-ups. Results are a snapshot by default — writers re-trigger `fetch` when they finish. Against the NodeGX backend, turning on the `Live` input keeps the results current automatically: the node opens a realtime (SSE) subscription to the collection and re-runs the query (debounced) whenever a matching record changes, so the server re-applies the real filter/sort/paging each time.
enrichment.whenToUse: Reading lists from a self-hosted backend. Turn on `Live` for a hands-off live list on a NodeGX backend; for Directus, pair with a Subscribe To Changes node instead. On the managed cloud backend prefer Query Records (DbCollection2), which keeps results live in-process.

ports.fetch: Signal; runs the query. Wire a mount signal or a refresh event here.
ports.live: Boolean, default false. On a NodeGX backend, keeps results live by re-running the query when records change (realtime SSE). No effect on backends without SSE realtime — use Subscribe To Changes there.
ports.records: The result array; feeds a Repeater like any items source.
ports.totalCount: Total matching records server-side, independent of paging — drive pagination from this.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Class selection, filter-value inputs, paging inputs and the `Live` toggle are generated from the backend schema and the query configuration (runtime-discovered); only the trigger/result surface is static. `Live` re-runs the existing query on each change, so filter/sort/limit stay authoritative on the server; bursts of changes coalesce into a single debounced re-fetch.
antiPatterns: Polling on a timer — turn on `Live` (NodeGX) or pair with Subscribe To Changes (Directus) instead.
Expecting `Live` to work against a backend without SSE realtime — only the NodeGX backend serves it.

ssr.note: A live subscription is meaningless in a server render and would leak a socket per request; the node activates in the browser after hydration.

dynamicPorts.description: Some ports are discovered at runtime from user code, parameters or connected components, and are pushed to the editor per instance; the static port list below is incomplete for such instances.

enrichment.summary: Subscribe To Changes (BYOB): emits a signal with the changed record whenever a backend collection changes.
enrichment.description: Live change feed for a self-hosted backend collection. The transport is chosen by backend type: Directus (and other BYOB REST backends) use the WebSocket interface (requires WEBSOCKETS_ENABLED); the NodeGX standalone backend uses Server-Sent Events (SSE), where the server matches the subscription filter and enforces per-record read permissions before delivery, and a `resync` event signals a gap (reconnect or slow-client overflow) with no replay. While `subscribed` is true, creates, updates and deletes made by any client fire the matching `created`/`updated`/`deleted` signal plus the generic `changed`, with the affected record(s) on the Event outputs. The connection authenticates with the backend's token (SSE passes it as a query param since EventSource cannot set headers), answers heartbeats, and reconnects after a drop — `subscribed` reflects the live state throughout. Delete events carry only primary keys, so `changedRecord` is null for deletes; `changedRecordId` is always populated.
enrichment.whenToUse: Reacting to remote changes without polling — most commonly re-triggering a Query Data `fetch` so a list stays current. Works against both Directus (WebSocket) and the NodeGX backend (SSE) with no wiring difference. Not for reading data itself (use Query Data) and not on the managed cloud backend (its Query Records keeps results live already). Client-only: it stays inert during server-side rendering.

ports.enabled: Boolean, default true; set false to close the subscription (and stop reconnect attempts) without removing the node.
ports.subscribed: True only while the subscription is confirmed live — false during connect, backoff and after fatal auth failure.
ports.created: Fires once per remote create batch, after the Event outputs have updated.
ports.updated: Fires once per remote update batch, after the Event outputs have updated.
ports.deleted: Fires once per remote delete batch; only keys are delivered, so `changedRecord` is null and `changedRecords` holds key strings.
ports.changed: Fires alongside every `created`/`updated`/`deleted` — and on a NodeGX `resync` — so wire this when any change should trigger the same reaction (e.g. a re-fetch).
ports.eventType: The last event kind as a string: 'create', 'update', 'delete', or (NodeGX SSE) 'resync'.
ports.changedRecord: First record of the last create/update batch (full record object); null for deletes.
ports.changedRecords: All records of the last batch; for deletes, an array of primary-key strings (string even for numeric keys).
ports.changedRecordId: Primary key of the first affected record as a string, across all three event types; the key field name comes from the synced schema.
ports.error: Last connection or protocol error object; cleared when a subscription (re)confirms. An invalid token is fatal — the node will not retry until a parameter changes.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: `backendId`, `collection` and `enabled` are dynamic inputs generated from the Backend Services metadata: the Backend dropdown lists configured backends (plus 'Active Backend'), and the Collection dropdown lists the selected backend's synced user collections. They appear once a backend with a synced schema exists; an authoring tool may not assume any collection values without that schema. The transport (WebSocket vs NodeGX SSE) is selected automatically from the backend's type — authors do not configure it.
patterns: Subscribe To Changes `changed` → Query Data `fetch` keeps a BYOB-backed list live without polling (Directus or NodeGX).
On a NodeGX backend, a 'resync' event also fires `changed`, so a re-fetch recovers the list after a reconnect or slow-client overflow.
`subscribed` → a status indicator's visibility shows users when live updates are active.
antiPatterns: Treating `changedRecord` as the full record on deletes — delete events carry only primary keys.
Polling a Query Data on a timer while this node is available — subscribe and refetch on `changed` instead.

enrichment.summary: Update Record (BYOB): writes changed property values onto an existing record in a self-hosted backend by id.
enrichment.description: When `update` fires, the record targeted by the node's id input is patched with the values on its schema-generated property inputs. `success` returns the updated `record`; `failure` a structured `error`; `loading` spans the request. As with all BYOB nodes, dependent Query Data results must be re-fetched explicitly.
enrichment.whenToUse: Editing records on a self-hosted backend. On the managed cloud backend use Set Record Properties (SetDbModelProperties).

ports.record: The record as returned by the backend after the update.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Class choice, the id input and per-property inputs are schema-generated (runtime-discovered).

dynamicPorts.description: Group/aggregate output ports are generated from the aggregation definition in the node parameters.

enrichment.summary: Aggregate Records: computes min/max/sum/avg/distinct over a database class server-side, inside a cloud function.
enrichment.description: Aggregate Records runs an aggregation query against a cloud database class without transferring the records. It only exists in the cloud runtime, so it is used inside cloud function components. Pick the class in `collectionName` (Class), optionally narrow the records with a visual or JavaScript filter, then declare named aggregates in the `aggregates` list: for each name you choose a property and an operation — Min/Max/Sum/Avg for number properties, Distinct for string properties — and get an output carrying the computed value. `fetched` (Success, signal) fires when results arrive; `failure` (signal) fires and `error` (string value) is set on failure. The node also fetches automatically when its configuration inputs change, unless an explicit fetch signal is connected.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it for counts, sums, averages and distinct-value lists over many records — computing these server-side is the point. To read the records themselves use DbCollection2 (Query Records); browser logic must reach this node through a cloud function called via CloudFunction2.

ports.fetched: Signal (displayed 'Success'); fires after the aggregate outputs have been updated with fresh results.
ports.failure: Signal; fires when the aggregation fails. Read `error` for the message.
ports.aggregates: Edit-only name list; each name creates a Property/Operation input pair and a result output. Names must not contain spaces or special characters.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Ports are generated from the node's parameters and the database schema: `collectionName` (edit-only class enum), a filter port set that mirrors Query Records (visual `visualFilter` with `qp-<name>` query-parameter inputs, or a JavaScript filter with `storageFilterValue-<name>` inputs), a `storageFetch` ('Do', signal) action input, and per aggregate name `aggprop-<name>`/`aggop-<name>` edit-only inputs plus an `agg-<name>` output typed number (Min/Max/Sum/Avg) or string (Distinct). When `storageFetch` is not connected, any change to class, filter or query parameters schedules a fetch automatically.
patterns: Request `receive` → `storageFetch`, `agg-<name>` → Response result inputs, `fetched` → Response `send`: a stats endpoint the browser calls with CloudFunction2.
antiPatterns: Querying all records with DbCollection2 and summing them in graph logic — aggregate server-side instead and return only the numbers.

dynamicPorts.description: Output ports mirror the parameters declared for the cloud function (one output per request parameter).

enrichment.summary: Entry point of a cloud function component: receives the call's parameters and fires Received to start the server-side flow.
enrichment.description: Request is the entry node of a cloud function — it only exists in the cloud runtime, and a component containing one becomes callable from the browser through a Cloud Function (CloudFunction2) node. Declare the function's parameters as a name list in `params`; each name becomes an output carrying the value the caller sent, and a matching `in-<name>` input appears on the browser-side caller. When a call arrives the node checks authentication (rejecting unauthenticated calls unless `allowNoAuth` is true), publishes each parameter, then fires `receive` (Received, signal) — wire that signal into your logic and end the flow at a Response node. The caller's identity, parameters and headers are also placed on a 'Request' model readable elsewhere in the function.
enrichment.whenToUse: Place exactly one at the start of every cloud function component. It is meaningless in browser components — there, use Component Inputs for inputs and CloudFunction2 to call the function.

ports.receive: Signal; fires once per incoming call, after authentication has been checked and all parameter outputs hold the call's values. Start the function's logic from here.
ports.allowNoAuth: Boolean value (default false). When false, calls without a valid user session are rejected before the graph runs.
ports.auth: Boolean value; true when the call carried a valid user session.
ports.userId: Value holding the authenticated caller's user id (undefined for unauthenticated calls); use it to scope queries to the calling user.
ports.params: Edit-only name list declaring the function's parameters; drives both this node's outputs and the caller's inputs.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Each name in the `params` stringlist becomes a runtime-registered output (stored as `pm-<name>`, type '*') holding that parameter's value from the current call. The same list is what CloudFunctionAdapter mirrors onto browser-side CloudFunction2 callers as `in-<name>` inputs, so editing `params` changes both sides.
patterns: `receive` → your logic → Response `send`: every cloud function is this shape; the reply is not sent until a Response node sends it.
`userId` → a query filter parameter: trust the session-derived id, never an id passed in `params`, for per-user data.
antiPatterns: Leaving `allowNoAuth` false and then calling the function from a logged-out browser session — the call is rejected before `receive` ever fires.

dynamicPorts.description: Input ports mirror the result values declared for the cloud function (one input per response value).

enrichment.summary: Exit point of a cloud function component: collects result values and sends the reply back to the caller.
enrichment.description: Response ends a cloud function — it only exists in the cloud runtime. Declare the function's result values as a name list in `params`; each name becomes an input to feed, and a matching `out-<name>` output appears on the browser-side Cloud Function (CloudFunction2) caller. Triggering `send` (Send, signal) replies to the pending call: with `status` 'success' (the default) it returns HTTP 200 with the collected result values, with `status` 'failure' it returns HTTP 400 carrying `errorMessage`, which the caller surfaces on its `error` output before firing `failure`. A function can contain several Response nodes — for example one success and one failure path — but exactly one should send per call.
enrichment.whenToUse: End every path through a cloud function with one. Without a `send`, the caller's request never completes. In browser components use Component Outputs instead.

ports.send: Signal input; sends the reply for the current call using the current status, result values and error message. Trigger it exactly once per call.
ports.status: Enum value 'success' or 'failure' (default 'success'); selects between a 200 reply with results and a 400 reply with `errorMessage`, and switches which inputs the editor shows.
ports.errorMessage: String value returned to the caller when `status` is 'failure'; it appears on the caller's `error` output.
ports.params: Edit-only name list declaring the result values; drives both this node's inputs and the caller's outputs.

enrichment.runtimeBehavior: Each name in the `params` stringlist becomes a runtime-registered input (stored as `pm-<name>`, type '*') collected into the success reply. Declared port groups make the ports conditional on `status`: `params` (and its `pm-` inputs) exist while status is 'success' or unset, `errorMessage` exists while status is 'failure'. CloudFunctionAdapter mirrors the union of all Response nodes' `params` onto the browser-side caller as `out-<name>` outputs.
patterns: Two Response nodes — one with status 'success', one with status 'failure' and an `errorMessage` — triggered from the two branches of a Condition: explicit success/failure replies.
Feed `pm-` inputs as values as your logic computes them; only `send` decides when the reply goes out.
antiPatterns: Finishing a function path without triggering any Response `send` — the browser-side caller hangs until the request times out.

enrichment.summary: Sends an email through the backend's configured SMTP server from inside a cloud function or workflow.
enrichment.description: Send Email is a server-side-only action node (it only runs inside a cloud function, never in a browser component). Wire `send` to fire it: it either renders one of the backend's built-in templates (Password Reset, Verify Email) against the `variables` object, or sends the raw `subject`/`text`/`html` inputs directly. The send is synchronous from the graph's point of view — `sent` or `failed` fires once the attempt (plus one automatic retry on transient failure) has finished. If the backend has no SMTP configured, or this component is somehow evaluated outside a nodegx-backend process, it fails loudly on `failed`/`error` — it never drops a send silently or queues it for later.
enrichment.whenToUse: Use it wherever a workflow needs to notify someone by email — a signup confirmation, an order receipt, an internal alert. Do not use it for the account password-reset/verify-email flows the backend already runs (BAK-002) — those are automatic; wire this node only for YOUR OWN application notifications.

ports.template: 'none' sends the Subject/Text/HTML inputs as-is; 'passwordReset'/'verifyEmail' render the backend's built-in templates instead and ignore Subject/Text/HTML.
ports.variables: An object of `{{name}}` values for template interpolation; only read when Template is not 'none'.
ports.send: Signal; fires the send attempt (with its one documented retry on failure).
ports.sent: Signal; fires once the send succeeded.
ports.failed: Signal; fires once the send failed (or immediately if email isn't available at all) — read `error` for why.
ports.error: The failure message, e.g. "Email is not configured for this backend..." — always a specific, actionable string, never a generic failure.

patterns: Request `receive` → Send Email `send` → Response `send`: a fire-and-notify cloud function, the same shape as the Request/Response round trip but with a side effect instead of (or in addition to) a computed value.
antiPatterns: Wiring this into a browser component — it has no effect there (no `_noodl_send_email` exists outside nodegx-backend) and the failure is confusing without knowing this node is cloud-only.
Assuming a fired `sent` means the recipient's inbox will show it soon — deliverability (SPF/DKIM/provider reputation) is the operator's SMTP provider's job, not this node's.

compatibility.$comment: Connection-compatibility semantics (SUB-005). The permitted-cast TABLE lives in the structural catalog (node-catalog.json#/typecasts) and is exported by the runtime itself (packages/noodl-runtime/src/nodelibraryexport.js); this file documents what the rules and each cast MEAN. scripts/node-catalog/merge.js fails if castSemantics ever drifts from the catalog table, and asserts every verifiedPairs entry against the rule implementation.

rules.gate: The editor permits a connection from output type F to input type T iff: F === T, or F === '*', or T === '*', or the typecast table has an entry {from: F, to: [... T ...]}. This is NodeLibrary.canCastPortTypes (packages/noodl-editor/src/editor/src/models/nodelibrary/nodelibrary.ts).
rules.wildcard: The type '*' (untyped) connects to and from anything. Many dynamic ports (Function/Expression outputs, Object properties) are untyped; the editor will accept any wiring to them, so correctness is the author's responsibility.
rules.delivery: The runtime performs no central value conversion on delivery: the raw output value is handed to the receiving input, whose setter coerces it (usually with plain JavaScript semantics). A permitted cast means 'the receiver knows what to do with this', not 'a converter runs on the wire'.
rules.allowConnectionsOnly: Ports typed with allowConnectionsOnly can only be driven by a connection, never set statically via parameters.
rules.allowEditOnly: Ports typed with allowEditOnly can only be set via parameters, never connected.

signalSemantics.firing: A signal output fires by sending the value true immediately followed by false (Node.prototype.sendSignalOnOutput, packages/noodl-runtime/src/node.js). A signal is a momentary event with no payload.
signalSemantics.receiving: A signal input triggers when its incoming value transitions to true (valueChangedToTrue) — it is edge-triggered, not level-sensitive. Holding a value at true does not re-trigger.
signalSemantics.suppression: A signal output that already fired in the current update cycle is suppressed from firing again until the cycle completes, preventing infinite loops within one frame.
signalSemantics.authoring: Wire signals to signals ('On Click' → 'Do'). Wiring a boolean to a signal input is legal and means 'trigger once on the rising edge'. Wiring a signal to a boolean input is legal and delivers a true-then-false pulse — useful for momentary states, wrong for latching ones.

castSemantics.string→number: Receiver coerces with JavaScript numeric conversion; non-numeric strings become NaN. Prefer a Number value if the source is numeric to begin with.
castSemantics.string→boolean: JavaScript truthiness: empty string is false, any other string (including 'false') is true.
castSemantics.string→image: The string is used as an image source: a project asset path or a URL.
castSemantics.string→color: The string is used as a color value: a project style-color name or any CSS color string ('#ff0000', 'rgba(0,0,0,0.5)').
castSemantics.string→enum: The string must equal one of the input's enum values (the value, not the label); anything else leaves the input unchanged or misconfigured.
castSemantics.string→textStyle: The string names a project text style.
castSemantics.string→dimension: Parsed as a CSS dimension: a bare number is treated as px; '50%' selects percent units.
castSemantics.string→array: The string is passed through unchanged. This cast exists for inputs that accept a named/shared collection id in place of an actual array (legacy Collection semantics). Do not expect JSON parsing.
castSemantics.string→object: The string is passed through unchanged. This cast exists for inputs that accept a Model/Object id in place of the object itself; the receiver resolves the id to the shared object.
castSemantics.boolean→number: true → 1, false → 0 by JavaScript coercion in the receiver.
castSemantics.boolean→signal: Edge trigger: the signal input fires once each time the boolean transitions from false to true. A boolean that is already true when connected does not fire it retroactively.
castSemantics.number→boolean: JavaScript truthiness: 0 and NaN are false, everything else true.
castSemantics.number→string: Decimal string form of the number.
castSemantics.number→dimension: The number is used as a pixel value.
castSemantics.date→string: The receiver converts the Date with JavaScript string coercion.
castSemantics.signal→boolean: The boolean input receives a true-then-false pulse each time the signal fires. Use for momentary behaviour only; the value does not stay true.
castSemantics.signal→number: The number input receives 1 then 0 each firing (boolean pulse coerced numerically). Rarely what you want; prefer States or a Counter.
castSemantics.cloudfile→string: The cloud file's URL as a string.
castSemantics.cloudfile→image: The cloud file is used as an image source (its URL).
castSemantics.textStyle→string: The text style's name as a string.
castSemantics.collection→array: Collection (legacy shared-list type) and array are interchangeable: the same underlying list object flows through unchanged.
castSemantics.array→collection: Array and collection (legacy shared-list type) are interchangeable: the same underlying list object flows through unchanged.

verifiedPairs.$comment: Sampled pairs asserted by scripts/node-catalog/merge.js against the gate rule + the catalog typecast table on every merge/check. 'permitted' must pass canCastPortTypes; 'rejected' must fail it.

permitted.note: rising-edge trigger — the idiomatic 'run when this becomes true'
must match an enum value exactly

rejected.note: numbers do not edge-trigger; go via boolean
no serialisation on the wire — extract a property instead
color is not readable back as a string
date only casts to string; use an Expression for timestamps
strings never trigger signals; go via boolean

examples.title: Hover highlight: Animate To Value driving a Color Blend
examples.description: The smooth-hover idiom: the card's `hoverStart`/`hoverEnd` signals flip a Switch, whose boolean (cast to 0/1) becomes the `targetValue` of Animate To Value — the node tweens `currentValue` toward the target whenever it changes. That animated 0→1 feeds Color Blend's `blendValue`, interpolating between its configured colors, and the result drives the card background. State, easing and color are three separate concerns in three small nodes.

examples.title: States: a collapsible panel with transitioned values
examples.description: States is the interaction state machine: the `states` parameter names the states ('collapsed,expanded'), the `values` parameter names the outputs each state assigns ('panelHeight'), and with `useTransitions` on, changing state tweens each value. `toggle` flips between two states; the per-value output drives the layout input (number→dimension cast gives pixels). Signal outputs per state and `stateChanged` are registered from the same configuration — this is the current replacement for the deprecated Animation node.

examples.title: Bring-your-own-backend: query, create, update, delete
examples.description: The noodl.byob.* family talks to a self-hosted backend with the same shapes as the classic cloud-data nodes but generic record objects: Query Data fetches on demand into `records` (no live re-query — refetch explicitly), Create/Update/Delete Record act on ids and fire success/failure, and every node exposes a `loading` boolean for progress UI. After any write, the query's `fetch` is re-triggered to refresh the list.

examples.title: Bring-your-own-backend: live list via Subscribe To Changes
examples.description: BYOB queries are snapshots — they only refresh when `fetch` fires. Subscribe To Changes closes that gap: it holds a WebSocket subscription on the collection and fires `changed` whenever any client creates, updates or deletes a record, so wiring `changed` → `fetch` keeps the list current without polling. `subscribed` drives a small 'live' indicator so users can see when realtime updates are active.

examples.title: Create a record with an uploaded file attachment
examples.description: The create-with-attachment flow: Open File Picker hands the picked browser file to Upload File, which stores it in cloud storage and outputs a `cloudFile`. Cloud File exposes that file's `url`, previewed in an Image (the cloudfile→image cast). When the upload succeeds, Create New Record (NewDbModelProperties) writes a new 'Attachment' record whose properties — including the file — are set on the node's schema-generated inputs. Database Config (DbConfig) is the singleton that points the app at its cloud backend; it has no wires, its presence and parameters configure the connection.

examples.title: Load, edit and save a single record
examples.description: The record-detail flow: a Record node (DbModel2) binds to one database object by `modelId` and exposes its properties as schema-generated outputs. The edit field is initialised from the record, and Save (SetDbModelProperties) writes the changed property back on click, targeting the same id. `stored` confirms the round trip. Property ports on both nodes come from the database schema — they are runtime-determined, wired here exactly as the editor would write them.

examples.title: One query, two tabs: client-side Filter Records views
examples.description: One Query Records fetch fans out into two Filter Records nodes — 'open' and 'done' — each feeding its own Repeater. The filtering happens client-side against the already-fetched array, so switching tabs costs nothing and both views stay live as the underlying query updates. Filter in the query itself only when the excluded data shouldn't reach the client at all.

examples.title: Add and remove a relation between records; delete a record
examples.description: Relations link records without embedding them: Add Record Relation points `modelId` (the owner) at `targetId` (the related record) on a named relation field, Remove Record Relation severs the same pair, and Delete Record removes a record entirely. All three act on ids delivered by wires — here from the enclosing component's inputs — and fire a confirmation signal (`relationAdded`, `relationRemoved`, `deleted`) or `failure` with `error`.

examples.title: CSS Definition: project stylesheet applied via class names
examples.description: CSS Definition injects the stylesheet in its `style` parameter into the page — it has no output ports; its presence is its effect. Visual nodes opt in through their `cssClassName` input. Use it for what node parameters cannot express (pseudo-selectors, keyframe animations, media queries); prefer node style parameters for everything they can express, since the editor cannot inspect CSS effects.

parameters.style:
.pulse-banner { animation: pulse 2s infinite; }
@keyframes pulse { 0% { opacity: 1; } 50% { opacity: 0.6; } 100% { opacity: 1; } }

examples.title: HTTP Request with scripted post-processing and error display
examples.description: HTTP Request (net.noodl.HTTP) fetches the `url` when `fetch` fires and delivers `response` (parsed body), `statusCode`, and either `success` or `failure` with `error`. The response is post-processed by a Script node (Javascript2), whose input/output ports are declared by its own code — here it reads `Inputs.response` and produces a `headline` output. Errors surface as a level: `failure` evaluates a Condition whose `result` shows the error text.

examples.title: Logic Builder: block-built logic with generated ports
examples.description: Logic Builder holds a visual block workspace (`workspace`) from which it generates JavaScript (`generatedCode`); the blocks' declared inputs and outputs become the node's ports, exactly like a Function node's script does. Here the generated logic turns a name into a greeting: the text input feeds the block-declared `name` input, `run` executes, and the block-declared `greeting` output lands in a Text. Use it where non-programmers must be able to read and edit the logic; use Function for anything a programmer maintains.

examples.title: REST node feeding a repeater
examples.description: The REST node wraps a request/response pair in two scripts: the request script assembles the call from the node's script-declared inputs, and the response script maps the payload onto script-declared outputs — here an `items` array. Ports come from those scripts (that is its dynamism). `fetch` on mount loads the list; `success`/`failure` sequence what follows. For a one-off GET without mapping scripts, HTTP Request is the lighter tool.

examples.title: Create a client-side object and bind to it by id
examples.description: Create New Object (NewModel) makes a fresh client-side object with the property values on its schema-declared inputs and outputs the new `id`. An Object node (Model2) bound to that id then exposes the object's properties reactively — the create node acts, the Object node observes. This id-handoff is the core client-data shape: writers and readers connect through ids, not direct wires.

examples.title: Repeater item writes back to its own record object
examples.description: Inside a Repeater item component, Repeater Item (For Each Actions) exposes `itemId` — the id of this row's object. Wiring it into Set Object Properties (SetModelProperties) `modelId` makes the write target exactly this row: toggling the checkbox stores `done` on the row's object, and every other node bound to that object updates. The row never needs to know which list it belongs to.

examples.title: Wizard step state shared via Component Object
examples.description: Component Object is per-component-instance shared state: every node in the same component instance — and, via the Parent variants, in its child components — reads and writes the same object without wires between them. The wizard holds `step` in its Component Object; the embedded controls component advances it with Set Parent Component Object Properties and reads it with Parent Component Object. Two wizard instances on one page would each have their own independent `step`, which is exactly what plain shared Objects would not give you.

examples.title: Settings form: the standard input controls bound to values
examples.description: One of each core control: Text Input's live string comes out of `onTextChanged`, Checkbox exposes `checked` (level) plus `onChange` (edge), Dropdown (net.noodl.controls.options) takes an items list and emits the selected `value`, Slider (net.noodl.controls.range) emits a numeric `value` between `min`/`max`, and a Radio Button Group reports the `value` of whichever child Radio Button is selected. Values flow into a live summary — no submit step needed for value binding.

examples.title: Run Tasks: batch-process an array with a worker component
examples.description: Run Tasks executes its `taskTemplate` component once per element of `items`, up to `maxRunningTasks` at a time, and fires `done` when the whole batch has finished. The worker is a plain component: it receives the item's properties through Component Inputs and reports completion through Component Outputs signals (success/failure), which Run Tasks consumes to schedule the next task. Here a fresh array is assembled with New Array and processed on click.

examples.title: Named shared array with insert, remove and clear
examples.description: A client-side list without a backend: an Array node (Collection2) binds to the named shared array 'todos' and feeds a Repeater. Add Item (CollectionInsert), Remove Item (CollectionRemove) and Clear (CollectionClear) mutate the same array by its `collectionId`; every node bound to that id — including the Array feeding the list — sees the change immediately. Ids on wires tie the writers to the store.

examples.title: Static array filtered and mapped into a list
examples.description: Local data without a backend: Static Array holds inline JSON, Array Filter narrows it with a per-item filter script, Array Map reshapes each element with a map script, and the result drives a Repeater. Filter and Map are non-destructive — they emit new arrays and leave the source untouched, so several differently-filtered views can share one source.

parameters.mapScript: map({ name: object.name, label: object.name + ' — $' + object.price })

examples.title: Server-side aggregation exposed as a cloud function
examples.description: Aggregate Records runs count/sum/min/max/average over a database class without transferring the records — it exists only in the cloud runtime, so the idiomatic shape is a small cloud function around it: Request triggers the aggregate's fetch, `fetched` sends the Response, and the aggregate results (outputs generated from the `aggregates` configuration) are returned as response params. The browser calls it like any cloud function and renders the statistic.

examples.title: Cloud function round trip: browser call → request → response
examples.description: A cloud function is a component that runs server-side: Request is its entry (its `params` become outputs carrying the caller's inputs; `receive` fires per invocation) and Response is its exit (its `params` become inputs; `send` returns them). In the browser, Call Cloud Function (CloudFunction2) names the function; the function's request params appear as inputs and its response params as outputs. Here two numbers are summed server-side: the browser sends a and b, the function computes with an Expression, and `sum` comes back on `success`.

examples.title: Cloud function that sends an email notification
examples.description: A cloud function that receives a recipient/subject/message from its caller and emails it through the backend's configured SMTP server. Request's `params` become this function's inputs; Send Email fires on `receive` and reports success/failure back to Response, which the caller reads as usual. This is the general-purpose shape for any application email (signup confirmations, receipts, alerts) — distinct from the backend's own automatic password-reset/verify-email flows (BAK-002), which never need a Send Email node.

examples.title: Function node: custom JavaScript with discovered ports
examples.description: The Function node (JavaScriptFunction) runs the JavaScript in `functionScript`. Its data ports do not exist until the script mentions them: reading `Inputs.x` creates an input named x, assigning `Outputs.y = …` creates an output named y, and calling `Outputs.done()` fires a signal output — this is why the catalog marks them runtime-determined. The script runs when `run` is triggered (or when connected inputs change, if `run` is unconnected). Here a button converts a text amount to a formatted price.

examples.title: Debounced autosave with timestamped status
examples.description: The debounce idiom: every keystroke fires Value Changed, whose signal restarts a 1.5-second Timer — the save only runs when the user pauses. The save Function stamps the moment; Date To String formats it, Unique Id issues a save id shortened by Substring, and String Format assembles the status line. Signals sequence the flow; values shape the display.

examples.title: Gate a button on all required checks, reveal a note on any optional one
examples.description: And and Or as pure boolean-value combiners over numbered inputs. Two required checkboxes feed an And node's "input 0" and "input 1"; its `result` drives the submit button's `enabled` as a level, so the button enables the instant both are ticked and disables again if either is cleared. Two optional email checkboxes feed an Or the same way; its `result` shows an explanatory note while at least one is ticked. No signals are involved — everything here is level logic.

parameters.label: I accept the terms of service

parameters.text: We will only email you what you asked for. Unsubscribe anytime.

examples.title: Quantity stepper: Counter with remapped and formatted readouts
examples.description: Two buttons drive a Counter up and down within limits. The count feeds three displays: a String Format caption ('{count} items'), a String Mapper that maps special values to words (0 → 'empty'), and a Number Remapper converting the 0–10 range into 0.2–1 opacity for a fill indicator. Counter holds the state; the display nodes are pure value-shaping between it and the UI.

examples.title: Toggle a details panel with a self-labelling button
examples.description: The standard show/hide toggle: one button flips a Switch, and everything else derives from the Switch's boolean `state` as levels — the details Group's visibility directly, the summary text's visibility through an Inverter (visible only while collapsed), and the button's own label through Boolean To String so the button always names what it will do next. Note the split of flow kinds: `onClick` → `flip` is a signal (momentary), while every `state`-derived wire is a value that holds its level.

parameters.text: 3 items — tap the button for a full breakdown.
2 × Coffee beans, 1 × Filter papers. Free shipping.

examples.title: Push and pop a Component Stack (wizard flow)
examples.description: Stack-style navigation: a Page Stack (Component Stack) named 'Checkout' hosts two components, defined in its `pages` parameter with `pageComp-<id>` entries mapping each page to a component in this file. Inside /Cart, a Push Component To Stack node (PageStackNavigate) pushes /Confirm with a transition when the Continue button is clicked. Inside /Confirm, a Pop Component Stack node (PageStackNavigateBack) pops back: the Back button triggers its plain `navigate` signal, while the Place-order button triggers the `backAction-confirmed` signal input declared via the `backActions` parameter — that same action surfaces as the `backAction-confirmed` signal output on the Push node in /Cart, where it fires an Event Sender. This is the round-trip: back actions are declared on the Pop node inside the pushed component and consumed on the Push node that pushed it.

examples.title: Show a popup and close it from inside with a close action
examples.description: The popup pair: a Show Popup node (NavigationShowPopup) opens the /Confirm Delete Dialog component as an overlay when the Delete-account button is clicked. The Close Popup node (NavigationClosePopup) lives INSIDE the popup component — it is the only way the popup ends itself. Its `closeActions` parameter declares 'confirm,cancel', which registers `closeAction-confirm` and `closeAction-cancel` signal inputs on Close Popup and matching signal outputs on the Show Popup node that opened it: the host reacts to `closeAction-confirm` without knowing anything about the dialog's internals. A close action both closes the popup and routes the outcome; plain `close` (not used here) would fire Show Popup's generic `Closed` output instead.

parameters.text: Delete your account? This cannot be undone.

examples.title: URL-driven detail page: Router, Page Inputs, Navigate To Path and External Link
examples.description: URL-style navigation end to end. A Router named 'Main' hosts /Home and /Product (its `pages` parameter is `{ routes, startPage }`); each page component is rooted by a Page node whose `urlPath` defines its URL pattern — /Product uses 'product/{productId}', so the id lives in the URL. On /Home, a Navigate To Path node (PageStackNavigateToPath) builds the URL from its `path` parameter: the '{productId}' placeholder becomes the `p-productId` input, set here as a parameter, and clicking the button pushes the compiled path into browser history, which the Router picks up. On /Product, a Page Inputs node declares `pathParams: "productId"` so the value parsed from the URL is exposed as its `pm-productId` output, wired into a Text. An External Link node (net.noodl.externallink) opens an outside URL in a new tab — external URLs never go through the Router.

examples.title: Router page navigation from a button
examples.description: URL-style navigation: a Router hosts the app's pages (each page is a component, configured in the Router's `pages` parameter), and a Navigate node (RouterNavigate) switches it. The Button's `onClick` signal triggers `navigate`; which page to go to, and any path parameters, are set on the Navigate node's parameters — those ports are created from the Router's page configuration at edit time, which is why they are runtime-determined in the catalog.

examples.title: List page: Repeater fed by Query Records
examples.description: The canonical data-list shape. Query Records (DbCollection2) fetches a database class and exposes the result on its `items` array output; the Repeater (For Each) consumes that array and instantiates its `template` component once per record. Each record's properties are delivered to the item component through Component Inputs whose names match the record's property names — the item component reads them like any other input. The Repeater and its item template component are separate components by design.

examples.title: Decoupled communication with Send Event / Receive Event
examples.description: Events carry a signal (and optional payload values) between components with no wire between them: every Receive Event listening on the same `channelName` fires when a Send Event on that channel sends. Here a toolbar button broadcasts 'RefreshRequested', and a separate component re-runs its data fetch when it receives the event. Use events when the sender must not know who reacts; for parent↔child data flow prefer Component Inputs/Outputs.

examples.title: Log in, show the user, log out
examples.description: The authentication triangle: Log In takes `username`/`password` values and a `login` signal, firing `success` or `failure` (+`error`). The User node is the session's single source of truth — its `authenticated` boolean and profile outputs update on login/logout, so UI binds to it rather than to the action nodes. Log Out ends the session from anywhere. Gate visible areas on `authenticated`, not on the login node's `success` pulse.

examples.title: Sign up, then set profile properties
examples.description: Sign Up creates the account and starts a session (`success` fires once the user is signed up and logged in). Custom profile fields beyond username/email/password are written afterwards with Set User Properties, whose property inputs are generated from the user-class schema — here `displayName` is set from the same form, triggered by the signup succeeding. Chain the signals: signup `success` → set-properties `store`.

examples.title: Validate an input before acting on a click
examples.description: The idiomatic gate shape: a Button click does not act directly — it evaluates a Condition. The Condition's boolean comes from an Expression that checks the text input's current value, so the same click either proceeds (ontrue) or reveals an error message (isfalse drives the error Text's visibility as a level, not a pulse). Note the two kinds of flow: text/booleans are values, onClick/eval/ontrue are momentary signals.

parameters.text: Please enter a valid email address.

examples.title: File picker with a shared accent color and a viewport-aware hint
examples.description: Three utility shapes in one small screen. A Color node is the single source of truth for the accent: its savedValue fans out to the title's text color and the button's background, so one edit restyles both. The Button's onClick fires Open File Picker's open — the dialog must come from a user gesture — and after a pick the file's name flows into a Text while success latches a Boolean (value pinned true) that reveals the result row as a level; cancelling the dialog fires nothing. Screen Resolution's width feeds an Expression (width < 600) whose boolean drives the compact hint's visibility, updating live as the window resizes.

parameters.text: Tip: rotate your device for a larger preview.

examples.title: Click counter with a latched Number and a Boolean flag
examples.description: The canonical per-instance counter: a Number node's savedValue feeds an Expression (count + 1) whose result loops back into the Number's value input. Because saveValue (Set) is connected, the incremented value is only committed when the Button's onClick fires — the latch is what makes the feedback loop safe. The count renders directly in a Text (number casts to string on delivery). A Boolean node shows the latch-a-signal-into-a-level shape: its value is pinned to true in parameters, the same click fires its Set, and its savedValue permanently reveals the hint text — a level, unlike the momentary click signal.

parameters.text: You have clicked at least once.

examples.title: Share a value between components with Set Variable and Variable
examples.description: The idiomatic shared-state shape, contrasting per-instance and app-wide storage. In the form component, a String node snapshots the text field: because its saveValue (Set) is connected, keystrokes only latch a pending value, and the Button click commits it. The String's stored signal then fires the Set Variable's do, writing the committed text into the app-wide variable 'userName' (setWith 'string' types the dynamic value input). In a completely separate component, a Variable2 node bound to the same name reads the value reactively — its changed/value update the greeting automatically whenever the variable is written, with no connection between the two components.

examples.title: Media card row: Columns layout with Image, Icon and Circle
examples.description: A card layout composed from the visual primitives: Columns (net.noodl.visual.columns) distributes its children by a layout string ('1 2' — the second column twice as wide), the Image shows a picture from a URL/asset on `src`, the Icon (net.noodl.visual.icon) renders a themed glyph, and the Circle doubles as a status dot whose `fillColor` is data-driven. Layout is containment; only the dynamic bits (image source, status color) are wired.

examples.title: Draggable chip that snaps back on release
examples.description: Drag is a visual container that makes its children draggable. Its `onStop` signal fires when the user releases; wiring it to the `snapToPositionX.do`/`snapToPositionY.do` signal inputs animates the chip back to the configured snap position (0,0 here) over the given duration. `positionX`/`positionY` report the live offset while dragging — here mapped into the label.

examples.title: Wrapper component: Component Children marks the insertion point
examples.description: Component Children is a placeholder with no ports: whatever children are given to an *instance* of the component are rendered where the placeholder sits. Here '/Media Frame' is a reusable framed panel — title bar on top, content slot below — and the consumer drops a Video inside its instance. The video's play/pause wiring lives at the consumer level; the frame knows nothing about its content.
